title: Guidance on Use of Artificial Intelligence-Based Tools in Practice Before the United States Patent and Trademark Office
author: United States Patent and Trademark Office

dom.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment

st.t: AI filings: Disclosure rules divide otherwise similar courts
st.an: The USPTO guidance accepts the cluster’s core approach: AI assistance does not transfer responsibility, and verification must substantively cover facts, evidence, citations and legal arguments. It materially extends that framework to patent practice by identifying a specific, conditional disclosure trigger when a submitted AI-drafted claim is known to lack significant human inventive contribution, rather than requiring blanket disclosure of AI use.
qs: Additionally, the party or parties should also perform an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances confirming all facts presented in the paper have or are likely to have evidentiary support and confirming the accuracy of all citations to case law and other references.

Thus, if an AI system is used to draft patent claims that are submitted for examination, but an individual listed in [37 CFR 1.56(c)](https://www.ecfr.gov/current/title-37/section-1.56#p-1.56(c)) has knowledge that one or more of the claims did not have a significant contribution by a human inventor, that  ( printed page 25615)  information must be disclosed to the USPTO.

st.t: Court responsibility: AI requires lifecycle supervision
st.an: The USPTO guidance supports the cluster’s core proposition by identifying confidentiality and privacy risks from third-party AI systems, endorsing human verification of AI-generated filing content, and treating existing professional rules as continuing safeguards. Its focus is narrower than the cluster’s full court-governance lifecycle, but it does not conflict with that broader framework.
qs: Other issues arise from seeking AI assistance by sharing sensitive and confidential client information to third-party AI systems, including those potentially located outside of the United States.[[9](#footnote-9-p25610)]  The legal community has recognized the need to identify and explore AI risks in legal proceedings.

st.t: Hallucination governance: Sanctions target inquiry failures
st.an: The USPTO guidance directly supports the cluster’s principal proposition: AI-assisted drafting is permissible, but human filers remain accountable for reasonable inquiry, verification, correction, candor and professional duties. It also supports relying on existing, technology-neutral rules without routine AI-use disclosure, while allowing disclosure when specifically requested or substantively required.

st.t: Legal copilot: Verification costs define practical value
st.an: The USPTO guidance directly supports the cluster’s copilot framing: AI may assist drafting, but existing professional duties, human review and responsibility remain controlling because outputs may omit, misstate or fabricate information. It reinforces verification requirements for facts, citations and legal arguments, while offering no empirical evidence on whether verification costs preserve or eliminate efficiency gains.
qs: Therefore, if an AI tool is used in drafting or editing a document, the party must still review its contents and ensure the paper is in accordance with the certifications being made.

Additionally, the party or parties should also perform an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances confirming all facts presented in the paper have or are likely to have evidentiary support and confirming the accuracy of all citations to case law and other references.

st.t: Professional governance: Existing duties need active AI scrutiny
st.an: The USPTO guidance directly supports the cluster’s proposition that existing professional rules remain the ethical foundation but require active AI-specific scrutiny. It applies those rules to confidentiality risks from third-party tools, practitioner education and mitigation, and reports verification requirements for AI-assisted filings without asserting a blanket new reliability regime.
qs: Other issues arise from seeking AI assistance by sharing sensitive and confidential client information to third-party AI systems, including those potentially located outside of the United States.[[9](#footnote-9-p25610)]  The legal community has recognized the need to identify and explore AI risks in legal proceedings.

st.t: Supervised AI: Verification may consume efficiency gains
st.an: The USPTO guidance directly supports the cluster’s core framing: AI assistance is permitted, but existing professional duties remain controlling, human review and substantive verification are mandatory, and confidentiality requires scrutiny of actual provider practices. It identifies potential efficiency gains but does not claim that verification necessarily eliminates them or provide empirical evidence resolving that trade-off.
qs: In order to obtain the knowledge necessary to make these certifications, the party presenting the paper must have reviewed and verified the paper and its contents.
Therefore, before using these AI tools, it is imperative for practitioners to understand an AI tool's terms of use, privacy policies, and cybersecurity practices.

st.t: Supervisory accountability: Verification must test substantive support
st.an: The USPTO guidance directly supports the cluster’s core proposition that AI assistance does not displace professional responsibility and that verification must test substantive support. It requires human review of AI-assisted submissions, including evidentiary support, citation accuracy and whether legal arguments are warranted, while applying existing confidentiality and candor duties. It does not materially extend the cluster’s specific emphasis on supervisory or institutional leadership.
qs: Therefore, if an AI tool is used in drafting or editing a document, the party must still review its contents and ensure the paper is in accordance with the certifications being made.

Additionally, the party or parties should also perform an inquiry reasonable under the circumstances confirming all facts presented in the paper have or are likely to have evidentiary support and confirming the accuracy of all citations to case law and other references.

st.t: Work redesign: Jagged capability demands selective deployment
st.an: The USPTO guidance supports selective, human-led deployment: it permits AI assistance and recognises potential task-specific benefits, while retaining responsibility with natural persons and requiring independent verification under existing professional duties. It adds domain-specific controls for patent practice, confidentiality and system access, but does not materially develop the cluster’s broader claims about organisational redesign or labour effects.

kp.k: Existing obligations govern AI without new substantive rules
kp.d: Applicable April 11, 2024, the USPTO guidance states that existing rules protect its ecosystem against potential AI risks. It explains their application to patent and trademark practice, including PTAB and TTAB proceedings, rather than creating new substantive requirements. The notice expressly lacks the force and effect of law and is not exhaustive.
qs: This guidance does not constitute substantive rulemaking and does not have the force and effect of law.
This guidance is not intended to announce any new USPTO practice or procedure and is meant to be consistent with current USPTO policy.

kp.k: AI expands drafting, research, and examination capabilities
kp.d: The USPTO describes existing AI-enabled prior-art searches by examiners and increasing practitioner reliance on AI for prior-art research, application review automation, and examiner insights. It identifies drafting specifications, claims, responses, and briefs as available capabilities. Lower costs, reduced barriers, and improved service quality and efficiency are presented as potential benefits, not quantified findings.
qs: Patent practitioners are increasingly relying on AI-based tools to research prior art, automate the patent application review process, and to gain insights into examiner behavior.

These tools have the potential to lower the barriers and costs of practicing before the Office as well as helping law practitioners offer services to their clients with improved quality and efficiency.

kp.k: AI drafting is permitted without blanket disclosure
kp.d: The guidance permits AI-assisted document drafting and imposes no general obligation to disclose its use to the USPTO. Exceptions include specific Office requests and use material to patentability. This absence of routine disclosure does not remove duties to review submissions, correct errors, competently represent clients, or consult them about the means of representation.
qs: The capabilities of these tools continue to grow, and there is no prohibition against using these computer tools in drafting documents for submission to the USPTO.
Nor is there a general obligation to disclose to the USPTO the use of such tools.

While those parties presenting a paper to the USPTO are under a duty to review the information in the paper and correct any errors, there is not presently a general duty to inform the USPTO that an AI tool was used in the drafting of the paper unless specifically requested by the USPTO.

kp.k: Human verification remains mandatory for AI-assisted submissions
kp.d: Under the guidance's application of 37 CFR 11.18(b), anyone presenting a paper, including an unrepresented applicant, remains responsible for its contents. Reasonable inquiry requires checking factual support, citations, and legal contentions rather than trusting AI output. The notice cites Mata v. Avianca as a sanctions incident involving fabricated citations and quotations, not as a measurement of model error rates. Errors and omissions must be corrected; violations can lead to striking papers, disciplinary referral, or termination of proceedings.
qs: In order to obtain the knowledge necessary to make these certifications, the party presenting the paper must have reviewed and verified the paper and its contents.
Simply relying on the accuracy of an AI tool is not a reasonable inquiry.
Upon review of the document drafted with the assistance of an AI tool, any errors or omissions in the document must be corrected.

kp.k: AI-generated claims require human inventorship scrutiny
kp.d: The notice explains that AI may introduce alternative embodiments not conceived by the listed inventors, requiring reassessment of inventorship and patentability. Each named inventor must significantly contribute to a claimed invention under the referenced Pannu factors. Information about AI use, including inputs and outputs, must be disclosed when material to patentability; the guidance does not impose disclosure merely because AI participated.
qs: For example, in patents and patent applications, all patent claims must have a significant contribution by a human inventor.
This could occur where an AI system assists in the drafting of the patent application and introduces alternative embodiments which the inventor(s) did not conceive and applicant seeks to patent.
Therefore, practitioners should carefully reevaluate that the appropriate inventors are listed on the patent application.

kp.k: Technical verification must precede patent filing
kp.d: Practitioners must check AI-drafted specifications and drawings for technical accuracy and compliance with 35 U.S.C. 112, modify claims into patentable form, and distinguish prophetic examples from actual working examples. The guidance warns that later corrections may introduce new matter and that correcting inaccurate foreign or international priority disclosures can jeopardize priority.
qs: Also, when AI tools are used to produce or draft prophetic examples, appropriate care should be taken to assist the readers in differentiating these examples from actual working examples.

Care should be taken to ensure that the disclosures of foreign or international patent applications drafted using AI tools, to which the U.S. patent application claims priority, are technically accurate to avoid loss of priority due to the filing of amendments to correct technical errors in the U.S. application.

kp.k: Automated prior-art submissions cannot replace individual disclosure duties
kp.d: AI can collect prior art and populate information disclosure statements, but the USPTO warns that unchecked automation could burden examiners with cumulative and irrelevant material. Reasonable inquiry includes reviewing each listed reference, removing clearly irrelevant and marginally pertinent cumulative information, and ensuring material information is not omitted. The duty of disclosure remains with the designated individuals, not the system.
qs: While AI could be attractive to some patent applicants and practitioners, the unchecked use of AI poses the danger of increasing the number and size of IDS submissions to the USPTO, which could
This duty cannot be transferred to another person or a computer system such as an AI tool.
Therefore, IDSs should also be reviewed to ensure that all material information is disclosed to prevent material information from being unknowingly omitted.

kp.k: Trademark evidence must reflect actual marketplace use
kp.d: AI-assisted trademark and TTAB filings require factual and legal verification across applications, maintenance filings, responses, and proceedings. The notice specifically warns against AI-generated specimens that do not show actual use in commerce and evidence that does not exist in the marketplace. Misstatements and irrelevant or unnecessarily cumulative material may also implicate the prohibition on filings for improper purposes.
qs: Particular care should be taken to avoid submitting any AI-generated specimens, which do not show actual use of the trademark in commerce, or any other evidence created by AI that does not actually exist in the marketplace.

kp.k: Signatures and accounts preserve natural-person oversight
kp.d: Although AI may assist mechanical filing tasks, required signatures must be personally entered by natural persons; an AI system cannot sign in its own name or apply another person's signature on their behalf. AI systems cannot obtain USPTO.gov accounts or be sponsored as support staff. These restrictions preserve human oversight rather than prohibiting all computer-assisted filing.
qs: The signer of the document cannot delegate this act to another person or entity.
Thus, it is not compliant with the rules to have the AI tool apply the signature of a person without being personally entered by that person.
Further, practitioners may not sponsor AI tools as a support staff individual to obtain an account.

kp.k: Automated access remains bounded by authorization and usage policies
kp.d: People using AI to interact with USPTO systems remain responsible for keeping access within their authorization. Policy violations may result in account revocation and criminal, civil, or administrative action. The notice warns that unusually high-volume automated database access violates website terms and recommends bulk data products for permitted data mining.
qs: Users should also be extremely careful when attempting to data mine information from USPTO databases.
Instead, users should consider using the USPTO's bulk data products for permitted and appropriate data mining efforts.

kp.k: Competence and supervision obligations extend to AI use
kp.d: The guidance applies existing USPTO duties of competence, diligence, client communication, and supervision to AI-assisted work. Practitioners must understand relevant technology's benefits and risks and maintain the legal, scientific, and technical knowledge required for representation. Supervisory responsibilities continue when practitioners and assistants use AI or third-party AI services; the notice distinguishes USPTO rules from the ABA Model Rules to which they correspond.
qs: Practitioners must keep abreast of the benefits and risks associated with any technology used to handle client matters before the USPTO.

Practitioners who supervise the work of other practitioners and non-practitioner assistants must ensure that the practitioners and staff under their supervision comply with the USPTO Rules of Professional Conduct when relying on AI tools and/or AI-related third party services.

kp.k: AI services introduce client confidentiality risks
kp.d: The USPTO identifies possible disclosure through prompts, retention, model training, third-party sharing, and security breaches. It warns that client information used in training may appear in outputs to others. Practitioners must safeguard confidentiality when buying commercial tools, commissioning proprietary systems, or using third-party storage, and understand terms, privacy policies, and cybersecurity practices before use. These are risk warnings rather than findings about every AI service.
qs: AI systems may retain the information that is entered by users.
If confidential information is used to train AI, that confidential information or some parts of it may filter into outputs from the AI system provided to others.
Therefore, before using these AI tools, it is imperative for practitioners to understand an AI tool's terms of use, privacy policies, and cybersecurity practices.

kp.k: AI infrastructure can trigger export and security restrictions
kp.d: The notice warns that overseas AI servers may export technical data in violation of applicable export controls, national-security requirements, or secrecy orders. Certain activities involving non-U.S. persons can constitute deemed exports even with domestic servers. It also emphasizes that a USPTO foreign filing license does not authorize exporting subject matter to prepare applications for U.S. filing, directing applicants considering such exports to BIS for appropriate clearances.
qs: Specifically, practitioners must be mindful of the possibility that AI tools may utilize servers located outside the United States, raising the likelihood that any data entered into such tools may be exported outside of the United States, potentially in violation of existing export administration and national security regulations or secrecy orders.

Even if the servers are located within the United States, certain activities related to the use of AI systems hosted by these servers by non-U.S. persons may be deemed an export subject to these regulations.
the export of subject matter abroad pursuant to a license from the USPTO, such as a foreign filing license, is limited to purposes related to the filing of foreign patent applications

kp.k: Automation does not excuse fraud or intentional misconduct
kp.d: The duty of candor and good faith extends to actions taken through automated tools. The USPTO states that it does not tolerate fraud or intentional misconduct in proceedings or access to its IT systems and monitors network traffic for unauthorized behavior. AI use does not displace individual accountability under existing rules and laws.
qs: The USPTO does not tolerate fraud or intentional misconduct in any manner in a proceeding before the Office or in connection with accessing USPTO IT systems.
The duty extends not only to the personal actions of these individuals, but also to the actions these individuals take with any automated tools, including AI tools.

cl.s: Concrete claim or prediction about how AI changes legal services, the legal profession, or legal markets (or, for a cross-domain source, its own domain)

pts.k: The USPTO describes expanding AI assistance in IP practice and predicts potential reductions in costs and barriers, alongside improvements in service quality and efficiency.
pts.d: The agency describes existing uses in prior-art research, application review, examiner-behavior analysis, and document drafting. It identifies tools capable of drafting specifications, Office-action responses, briefs, and claims with less human involvement. Cost and quality improvements are framed as potential benefits, not measured outcomes. Patent practitioners participating in the September 2023 AI/ET Partnership panel likewise suggested that AI could simplify prior-art searches, claim charting, and document review, while emphasizing human verification.

pts.k: AI-assisted drafting does not remove human responsibility for verification or compliance.
pts.d: The USPTO permits AI-assisted drafting but states that the person presenting a paper remains responsible for its contents. Its guidance requires review of facts, legal arguments, citations, and omissions under existing certification and candor rules. The practical model is assistance with human oversight, rather than direct reliance on autonomous output. The agency cites fabricated citations and quotations in AI-assisted litigation filings as an example of risk and warns of sanctions under USPTO rules.

pts.k: AI-generated patent content may change inventorship and patentability issues, requiring additional substantive review.
pts.d: The USPTO warns that AI drafting may introduce embodiments not conceived by the named inventors, making human contributions and disclosure obligations material. Practitioners must verify technical accuracy and statutory compliance before filing: subsequent corrections may constitute new matter, and errors in priority applications may jeopardize priority. These are conditional risks, not reported incidence rates.

pts.k: Automated prior-art collection and form population may increase irrelevant submissions and examination burdens.
pts.d: The USPTO states that AI can collect prior-art references and populate Information Disclosure Statement forms. It warns that unchecked use could increase submission volumes and burden examiners with cumulative or irrelevant information. Human review must cover each cited reference, not only the form, while ensuring material information is not omitted. The duty of disclosure cannot be transferred to an AI system.

pts.k: AI creates specific risks for trademark evidence and the integrity of filings.
pts.d: The USPTO cautions that AI-generated specimens may not demonstrate actual marketplace use. It also warns that inaccurate, irrelevant, or unnecessarily cumulative AI-generated material may cause delay or increase proceeding costs. Trademark and TTAB filings therefore require careful human review and evidentiary support.

pts.k: AI may automate mechanical filing tasks, but cannot replace the natural person responsible for signatures and authorized system access.
pts.d: The agency identifies potential automation of form completion, website information access, and uploads. Existing requirements prohibit delegating personal signature entry to AI and prevent AI systems from obtaining their own USPTO accounts or being sponsored as support staff. Users remain responsible for access limits. High-volume automated database access may violate website terms; the guidance recommends bulk data products for appropriate mining.

pts.k: Using third-party AI can expose confidential client information and create export-control and national-security risks.
pts.d: The USPTO identifies possible retention, model training, onward disclosure, and data breaches involving information entered for searches or drafting. Confidential information used in training may appear in outputs to others. Overseas servers and some access by non-U.S. persons can implicate export restrictions. The agency consequently emphasizes vendor diligence, confidentiality safeguards, and supervision of practitioners and assistants. These are prospective risk mechanisms, not documented breach rates.

cl.s: Evidence basis offered for the claim (data, benchmarks, cases, experience, authority, or none)

pts.k: The evidence consists principally of agency experience, stakeholder discussion, examples of tools, a sanctions case, and existing legal authority—not quantitative performance or market research.
pts.d: For current capabilities, the USPTO cites its PE2E AI search features, with notices from January and November 2022, the September 2023 AI/ET panel, and vendor examples for IDS automation. It cites Mata v. Avianca as a concrete sanctions incident involving fabricated citations and quotations, not a measured hallucination rate. Its account of obligations relies on federal regulations, statutes, manuals, account agreements, and earlier inventorship guidance. The agency's conclusion that existing rules address AI risks rests on stakeholder engagement and review of those rules. No quantified productivity gains, cost savings, adoption rates, or forecasts of legal employment are supplied.

cl.s: Stated or implied timeframe, conditions or qualifications under which the claim holds

pts.k: The guidance applies from April 11, 2024; capabilities are described as current or growing, while benefits and many risks are conditional and undated.
pts.d: The document offers no forecast horizon for cost reductions or broader market change. It describes existing rules as sufficient at the time of publication and commits to continued study. It is nonbinding guidance, not substantive rulemaking. There is no general duty to disclose AI-assisted drafting, but disclosure can be required when requested by the USPTO or when AI use is material to patentability. Permissible use remains subject to human verification, competence, candor, confidentiality, signature, and access requirements.

cl.s: Who is affected and how (market segment, role, firm type, clients, or the public)

pts.k: The source concerns the USPTO ecosystem: practitioners, applicants, inventors, trademark owners, tribunal parties, support staff, clients, and examiners.
pts.d: Patent and trademark practitioners may gain drafting and research assistance but retain verification, confidentiality, and supervisory duties. Applicants and clients may benefit from lower barriers and costs, while facing risks to patent rights, evidence integrity, and confidential information. Unrepresented filers also fall within the paper-presentation certification rules. Examiners gain AI search tools but could face increased irrelevant submissions. The source does not distinguish law-firm sizes, predict staffing changes, or quantify access-to-justice effects; its claims about lower barriers concern participation in the IP system.
